Vessel of Honor
vĕs´sĕl ŭv ŏn´ẽr
n. phrase (a container set apart for the master's use — Paul's figure for a believer purged and made fit for service)
Greek skeuos, any implement or container, used of a ship's gear, a household pot, the body, and a person; and time, honour, price. The vessel is defined by what it holds and whom it serves, not by its material.

Biblical Definition

The vessel of honour is the believer fit for use: “in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and of silver, but also of wood and of earth; and some to honour, and some to dishonour. If a man therefore purge himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honour, sanctified, and meet for the master's use, and prepared unto every good work” (2Ti 2:20–21). The potter's right is asserted: “Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?” (Rom 9:21). Saul of Tarsus is named one: “he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles” (Act 9:15). And the material is deliberately cheap: “we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us” (2Co 4:7).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines vessel as a cask or utensil proper for holding liquors and other things; and, in Scripture, a person; and honor as the esteem due or paid to worth, and a mark of high estimation.

expand to see more

VESSEL, n. A cask or utensil proper for holding liquors and other things, as a tun, a pipe, a puncheon, a hogshead, a barrel, a firkin, a bottle, a kettle, a cup, a bowl.

4. In Scripture, a person; the vessel of God's mercy or wrath.

HONOR, n. The esteem due or paid to worth; high estimation.

2. A testimony of esteem; any expression of respect or of high estimation by words or actions.

Key Scripture

2Ti 2:20 — "But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and of silver, but also of wood and of earth; and some to honour, and some to dishonour."

2Ti 2:21 — "If a man therefore purge himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honour, sanctified, and meet for the master's use, and prepared unto every good work."

Rom 9:21 — "Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?"

Act 9:15 — "But the Lord said unto him, Go thy way: for he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel:"

2Co 4:7 — "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us."

Modern Corruption

Honour is read as the vessel's material, and the passage says the gold and the clay can each be either.

expand to see more

Second Timothy 2:20 lists four materials and two uses, and the two lists do not line up. Gold and silver, wood and earth; some to honour, some to dishonour. Nothing in the sentence says the gold vessels are the honourable ones. In a great house a gold cup may be used for something shameful and a clay pot may serve the master's table, and verse 21 makes the distinction turn on one thing only: if a man therefore purge himself. The honour is a matter of cleanness and availability, not of endowment, which is why the verse is such a rebuke to churches that rank their members by gift.

Second Corinthians 4:7 goes further and makes the cheap material the point. The treasure — the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ, from the previous verse — is carried in earthen vessels that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us. A clay pot does not compete with what it holds. Paul then lists what earthen vessels look like in ministry: troubled, perplexed, persecuted, cast down, bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus. The fragility is the design, so that nobody mistakes the container for the contents.

Romans 9:21 supplies the sovereignty underneath and it must be stated without softening: the potter has power over the clay, of the same lump, to make one vessel unto honour and another unto dishonour. That is a hard doctrine and the Reformed have held it because Paul did. But its setting is a chapter that ends in mercy on vessels prepared for glory, and its practical use in 2 Timothy 2 is a command, not a fate: purge yourself. The potter's sovereignty and the man's responsibility to be clean are put in the same Bible by the same apostle, and the vessel is not invited to resolve the tension, only to be fit for use.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek skeuos (G4632), a vessel, implement; time / atimia (G5092, G819), honour / dishonour; ekkathairo (G1571), to purge out; ostrakinos (G3749), earthen, of clay.

expand to see more

Greek skeuos eis timen (G4632, G5092) — a vessel unto honour; 2 Timothy 2:20–21, Romans 9:21–23.

Greek skeuos ekloges (G1589) — a chosen vessel, a vessel of election; Acts 9:15 only.

Greek ostrakinois skeuesin (G3749) — earthen vessels; 2 Corinthians 4:7, 2 Timothy 2:20.

Usage

"“Some to honour, and some to dishonour” — and the materials do not decide it."

"“If a man therefore purge himself” — the one condition given."

"“This treasure in earthen vessels” — the cheap material is the design."
